transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-06
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~63 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marta (Arcturus Head ML), Ethan (Arcturus Infra), Solomon (CTO)

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a deep technical review on quantization, priya will walk through our bench and some tradeoffs, i'm alex from Redwood, AE, and priya SE.
[00:12] Marta: thanks alex, we're mainly looking at lowering cost for our inference fleet, we run a 13B model right now across a mix of A100 and some 80GB Ampere nodes, and we want to see if INT8 or fp8 or GPTQ can get us to 3x cost reduction without dropping accuracy on our customer prompts.
[00:28] Priya: great, that's exactly what we wanted to cover. quick agenda: accuracy/regression, perf (latency/throughput), kv caching behavior, batching changes, and deployment constraints for VPC / on-prem.
[00:40] Ethan: quick infra note, our on-prem boxes are mostly H100 80GB and a couple of A100 40GB, connected over 100gig. we use k8s with a custom nodepool, and we do not want to modify kernel params often.
[00:55] Priya: ok makes sense. first, high level on quant approaches: INT8 PTQ (post training quant) is fastest to deploy but has risk of larger accuracy regressions on some layers; FP8 gives you smaller regressions and is good for LLMs that have sensitive layernorms but requires hardware / runtime support. GPTQ (layerwise rounding + per-channel) is strong for 8-bit-ish compression and keeps quality often better than naive PTQ. AWQ is a newer approach that tends to give lower perplexity on many LLMs while remaining fast for inference \u2014 implementation details vary.
[01:30] Solomon: can you remind us what AWQ stands for? I keep seeing it in papers but not the acronym expansion.
[01:36] Priya: sure, AWQ = Adaptive Weight Quantization (informal naming in community) \u2014 it's a blend of mixed-precision per-block with clever rounding heuristics. not an official standard, but the library (awq) implements it.
[01:48] Marta: ok show us numbers, we care about top-line perplexity/accuracy on our evals and then also 95th perc latency.
[01:55] Priya: right, i'll summarize our internal microbench: we ran the 13B LLM on a mix of H100 and A100. baseline fp16 latency for 1-2 token streaming is ~42ms on H100 for our prompt distribution, throughput at steady-state with batching of 8 is ~150 tokens/s. GPTQ (8-bit) produced a 1.8% token-level perplexity increase on our test set, AWQ produced 0.9% increase, INT8 PTQ naive produced 3.6% \u2014 these are approximate and model dependent.
[02:30] Ethan: interesting \u2014 the AWQ number looks promising. how about token-level latency for kv-cache heavy workloads? our app uses long dialogs and we rely on KV cache to avoid recompute.
[02:42] Priya: good q. quantized models typically reduce raw compute time but can introduce extra memory bandwidth due to dequant/decompress on the fly. on H100 with our runtime, AWQ had similar KV cache hit behavior to fp16, but batch tail latency for cache-warmed requests increased ~5-8ms compared to fp16 because of dequant overhead when reading keys/values into compute. GPTQ had slightly more overhead (~10-12ms) in our runs because of its packing layout. INT8 naive was the worst due to mismatched kernels.
[03:15] Marta: so we would see small tail latency increases; our SLO is 99p < 120ms, so 8-12ms is probably acceptable if we get the cost wins.
[03:25] Alex: yes and important to note Redwood can route by policy \u2014 we can keep high-sensitivity traffic on fp16 or fp32 models and route bulk inference to quantized variants automatically. fallback is in platform.
[03:38] Ethan: about batching: we currently have dynamic batching enabled, heavy real-time chat where batch sizes rarely exceed 6. does quantization change batching benefits?
[03:46] Priya: quantization reduces per-token compute so it can reduce the marginal benefit of batching in some regimes \u2014 but in practice with kernels optimized for int8/awq you still get better throughput when you batch. the sweet spot shifts: on H100 batching 1->4 gives large latency improvement for fp16, for AWQ the curve is slightly flatter; so smaller batches are relatively better with AWQ than naive INT8.
[04:14] Solomon: any concerns about KV cache format compatibility? we use a custom KV cache in our infer stack.
[04:20] Priya: yes, compatibility is important. Redwood's runtime stores KV in a compressed layout; for quantized we kept keys in fp16 in our last prototype and only quantized weights. that keeps cache compatibility and avoids re-quantizing cache values on the fly. we can do that for Arcturus to minimize changes.
[04:38] Marta: that sounds safe. what about quantization-induced hallucinations or accuracy regressions on certain prompt categories \u2014 like math or code? we've seen regressions even when perplexity changes are small.
[04:50] Priya: absolutely. perplexity is a proxy but not perfect. we recommend running a representative eval set per workload: code, math, instruction-following, etc. AWQ often preserves tricky behaviors better than naive int8, but GPTQ sometimes preserves token distribution well too; it depends on layerwise sensitivity. we also run synthetic prompts targeting layernorm, softmax sensitivity to detect regressions.
[05:18] Ethan: can you share the test harness? we want to run the same bench in our env.
[05:22] Priya: yes, next steps i'll share a reproducible bench: script, dockerfile, and the AWQ/GPTQ conversion steps. note: GPTQ conversion can be long \u2014 sometimes hours for 13B depending on CPU. AWQ conversions are often faster but still nontrivial.
[05:36] Alex: there's a tradeoff operationally \u2014 if conversions are long, Redwood can preconvert and host a dedicated variant or we can do conversion as part of the customer pilot.
[05:46] Marta: on prem constraints: we cannot open outbound to internet from the cluster. how does conversion work then?
[05:52] Priya: two options: 1) conversion on an air-gapped machine using the same dockerized toolchain we provide; 2) Redwood does conversion in a secured environment and we ship a tarball of converted weights that you import. both are possible and we've done both for other customers.
[06:10] Solomon: any KMS/secret concerns when shipping weights? we need signing and integrity checks.
[06:15] Alex: yes Redwood supports artifact signing and secure transfer; for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS or provide checksums and signature files. we also keep audit logs for import/export operations.
[06:28] Ethan: about hardware support \u2014 FP8 requires hardware/driver support, do our H100s support fp8 execution?
[06:35] Priya: H100 does support some 8-bit float formats with recent drivers, but full fp8 performance depends on runtime kernels. Redwood's runtime has experimental fp8 paths but they're less mature than AWQ/int8 paths; we usually recommend AWQ/GPQ for best balance unless the customer has validated fp8 on their stack.
[06:57] Marta: can you summarize the recommended path for us?
[07:00] Priya: recommended: run AWQ conversion + Redwood microbench on your eval set (low conversion time, good accuracy retention). If AWQ meets your accuracy/latency targets, pilot with Dedicated or Private deployment. If AWQ fails for a narrow set of tasks, consider GPTQ for those specific model variants or keep those requests pinned to fp16.
[07:20] Ethan: about runtime metrics: what counters should we look at for regressions?
[07:25] Priya: track token-level perplexity, end-to-end 95/99 latency, KV cache hit/miss rates, dequant overhead (ms per token), memory bandwidth, and errors like NaNs or inf. also track qualitative evals.
[07:40] Alex: note we can add canary routing by prompt type in Redwood console, and rollback if quality drops beyond a threshold.
[07:48] Marta: any gotchas on model parallelism and quantization? we use tensor-parallel across 2 GPUs for 13B.
[07:54] Priya: yes model parallel / TP requires handling quantized shard layouts precisely. GPTQ packings sometimes assume certain shard shapes; AWQ is more flexible in our tests but you should run conversion with the same TP config. conversion tools often need to be run with the same TP topology or you have to re-shard.
[08:18] Ethan: ok, for our pilot we will share the topology file.
[08:22] Priya: perfect. quick demo of microbench highlights: (Priya shares screen) baseline fp16: 42ms single-token, AWQ: 36ms, GPTQ: 34ms but GPTQ showed a slightly worse perplexity cluster on code prompts, AWQ: 0.9% perplexity increase, GPTQ 1.8%.
[09:00] Marta: how consistent are those numbers across H100 vs A100?
[09:05] Priya: on H100 we saw AWQ slightly better latency due to faster tensor cores; on A100 it's similar but gap narrows. packing formats for GPTQ were less optimal on A100 in our runs.
[09:22] Solomon: what about runtime memory \u2014 peak GPU memory? does quantization reduce peak to allow bigger batches?
[09:30] Priya: quantized weights drastically reduce model size so you can fit larger batch / longer context sometimes. but runtime also needs extra workspace for dequant and some kernels. net memory reduction varied: AWQ gave ~30-40% model size reduction and ~20-30% peak GPU memory reduction in our tests, which allowed increasing batch from 8->12 in some configs.
[09:58] Ethan: do you have recommendations on profiling tools? we use nsight and our own prometheus hooks.
[10:03] Priya: nsight is good for kernel-level hotspots; we send perf hooks from Redwood runtime as Prom metrics \u2014 dequant time, kernel time, memory copies. we'll share the prometheus dashboard template.
[10:18] Marta: any known accuracy regressions for instruction-following models? we've seen hallucinations increase a bit with some int8 conversions.
[10:26] Priya: yes, instruction-following tasks can be sensitive. AWQ tends to preserve behavior better; also temperature/decoding tweaks can mitigate hallucinations. for critical prompts, keep a canary route on fp16.
[10:40] Alex: i want to call out we helped another customer (pseudonym Nova) run a mixed deployment: Awq for bulk plus fp16 for canary \u2014 they got 2.7x cost savings with no customer-facing diffs after 2 weeks of canary.
[10:58] Marta: good to hear. about conversion time: you said GPTQ can take hours \u2014 what's typical for 13B on our infra?
[11:05] Priya: on 32 vCPU machine with SSD it can be 2-6 hours; on beefier CPU it's faster. AWQ conversions often <1 hour for 13B. exact depends on shards and TP.
[11:18] Ethan: and does Redwood provide tooling to convert inside our air-gapped env?
[11:22] Priya: yes docker image + conversion script; we'll share offline.
[11:28] Solomon: licensing / IP concerns \u2014 can we run conversions locally and not send models to Redwood?
[11:33] Alex: absolutely, we support fully private conversions and you can run everything in your VPC. Redwood's Private deployment model supports that.
[11:45] Marta: last technical Q: what about mixed-precision on a per-layer basis? do you recommend per-layer fp16/awq mix?
[11:52] Priya: yes per-layer mixed precision is often best: keep first/last layers and projection layers in fp16, quantize the large MLP and attention weights. AWQ supports per-block settings. GPTQ can also keep certain layers at higher precision. this reduces regressions while retaining most memory savings.
[12:10] Alex: ok let's recap next steps briefly.
[12:13] Priya: will share AWQ/GPTQ benchmark scripts and results, plus dashboard templates.
[12:18] Alex: i'll send pilot pricing and Dedicated/Private options.
[12:22] Marta: we will share eval prompt set and infra topology.
[12:26] Ethan: we will confirm availability for kickoff week of 2027-12-13.
[12:30] Alex: perfect, thanks everyone. any final quick Qs?
[12:35] Marta: no, thanks \u2014 this was helpful.
[12:38] Solomon: thanks all.
[12:40] (call ends)
